title: [Cloudflare] What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026
summary: The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event.In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters.Disruptions at a glanceBetween July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption.In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five. Power failure was a leading cause of disruptionsThe Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data. Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns. In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3. Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%. Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country.Cloudflare Radar - Traffic volume by autonomous systemOn July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. As discussed in more detail below, geopolitical conflict remains a major driver of Internet disruptions. These incidents also show how conflict, energy infrastructure, and Internet connectivity are fundamentally intertwined.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficCloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficAlso of note: on August 13, a cooling system failure at a data center in the U.S. city of Phoenix caused a near-total drop in Internet traffic from Namecheap (AS22612). Outages such as these will be important to watch as the role of cooling systems becomes increasingly critical.Beyond the larger outages in Cuba, Honduras, and Ukraine, power-related disruptions also appeared across a wide range of countries, including Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Some of these events were caused by sudden failures, while others, such as planned load-shedding in Eswatini, reflected deliberate efforts to manage constrained power supply. Their scale and duration varied, but together they point to the same underlying dependency: when power systems become unstable, Internet connectivity often becomes unstable with them. In total, Radar observed 14 power-related disruptions across 10 countries during the quarter.The physical world takes the virtual world offlineLast quarter, Radar reported on the impact of Super Typhoon Sinlaku, as it moved through the Mariana Islands, knocking out power and, in turn, Internet connectivity in Guam, where HTTP traffic took four days to return to typical levels.Super Typhoon Bavi followed Sinlaku by less than three months, giving Guam two major storm-related connectivity disruptions in a single year. Officials appeared to take earlier preparedness steps ahead of Bavi, including declaring a state of emergency before peak storm conditions. Even so, the storm caused widespread power outages. The Guam Power Authority reported that strong winds brought down key transmission lines, leaving only about 25% of distribution feeders online at one point. From a connectivity perspective, the outcome was familiar: widespread power outages, downed transmission lines, and a multi-day recovery period for Internet traffic.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficIn Japan, an earthquake of similar magnitude, 7.1, prompted evacuation orders affecting roughly 150,000 people in Kumamoto. The impact on Internet connectivity primarily appeared in desktop traffic, while mobile traffic remained largely unaffected.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP requests time series for Kumamoto, JapanIn Colombia, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake in August caused building collapses, injuries, mass evacuations, and a four-and-a-half-day Internet disruption. Damage to fiber-optic infrastructure, compounded by the wider earthquake aftermath, drove a significant drop in traffic from Colombia Telecomunicaciones (AS3816).Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficFinally, in Nepal, sudden flash floods swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems on August 26, affecting communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. The flooding damaged homes, infrastructure, and essential services, including power, which in turn disrupted regional Internet connectivity. The outage recorded on Radar lasted two hours, during which HTTP traffic dropped by up to 18%.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficExam shutdowns continue in IraqGovernment-directed shutdowns were the largest cause of disruptions in Q3, the majority of which occurred in Iraq with separate scheduled shutdowns occurring throughout the quarter. The shutdowns took place on a strict schedule 03:30–04:00 UTC, lasting about 15-90 min each. The majority occurred between August 26 and September 28, with three occurring between July 1 and 8.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficPer Internet Society Pulse, “In a video message, Minister Mustafa Sanad, Iraq's Minister of Communication, confirmed the shutdown and vowed to develop a digital system that would eliminate the need for centralized exam distribution and, by extension, the need to shut down Internet access on exam days.” Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor the country’s networks as the development of the new system progresses.Notably, Syria and Sudan, two countries that have also frequently used exam-related Internet shutdowns in recent years, did not record similar disruptions this quarter. However, this likely reflects differences in exam calendars rather than a clear shift in policy. Radar will continue to monitor whether future national exam periods bring renewed shutdowns in either country.Disruptions coincide with political events In Ethiopia, renewed conflict in the Tigray region was accompanied by a government-directed Internet shutdown that lasted 10 days. Traffic dropped by 100%, signaling a full-scale shutdown.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficThe disruption revived memories of the extensive blockade imposed during Ethiopia’s civil war from 2020 to 2022, when Tigray was largely cut off from telecommunications, electricity, banking services, fuel, and humanitarian aid (France24), which the World Health Organization described as a “de facto blockade.” Although this latest outage appears to have remained localized to Tigray, its impact was still visible in country-level traffic, with HTTP traffic falling by up to 30%.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficOn September 19, during nationwide elections, fiber-optic cable damage in Russia’s Far East caused regional connectivity disruptions affecting Chukotka, Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka Krai, and Sakhalin Oblast. Rostelecom described the incidents as deliberate damage to backbone fiber lines and said connectivity was restored using backup channels. Radar data alone cannot determine whether the cable damage was related to the elections, but the timing is notable.Cloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficCloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficCloudflare Radar - HTTP trafficA quarter shaped by shutdowns and power outages, but also resilienceAcross Q3 2026, government-directed shutdowns were the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by Iraq’s exam-related shutdowns. Power outages were close behind, affecting networks across Cuba, Honduras, Ukraine, Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Natural disasters and conflict added another layer of disruption, reminding us that Internet resilience depends on far more than routers and cables. It depends on electricity, physical infrastructure, policy decisions, and the ability of networks to route around failure.Radar also observed outages inside individual networks, including One Communications (AS19863) in Guyana following a cable cut, MEO (AS3243) in Portugal following a reported “mass attack”, Digicel Haiti (AS27653), TurkNet (AS12735) in Turkey, and Fanap Telecom (AS206065) in Iran.Each of these events demonstrates the Internet’s fragility, but also its resilience. Many disruptions were brief: 14 saw traffic return to typical levels in under an hour, and 16 recovered in less than three hours. But short outages can still have real consequences for the people affected, especially during storms, earthquakes, conflict, or political unrest. Access to the Internet is often access to information, coordination, safety, and help.Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor Internet disruptions around the world and share what we see from Cloudflare’s global network. Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

title: [Cloudflare] Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
summary: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%.Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest.A request for part of a fileAn HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header:GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range:HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it.The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it.The range-size problemCloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration.The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone.The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key.This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range.The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology.Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently.Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers.Fixed-size cache chunksThe fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk!For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client.For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250.This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins.Coordinating cached and in-flight dataParsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress.At a high level, the edge:Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata.Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory.Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges.Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata.Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response.This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range.If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files.The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully.Validate before composingComposed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests.The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions.Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly.The resulting behavior is standard HTTP:A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range.An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable.A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation.What changed in productionBefore opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most.Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us.R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw:Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses.Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day.Getting startedOnce the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules. Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination.Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object:Progressive and seekable video such as MP4Resumable large downloadsSoftware distributions and package repositoriesDisk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objectsAI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifactsClients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger fileWe intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules.This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful.To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" }. Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.

title: [Cloudflare] Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
summary: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography.While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography.Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later.For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work.The evolution of GeoKey ManagerCloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (TLS) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager. This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network.GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key.That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel. This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries.Global ciphertext, regional key unwrappingIn its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all of them depend on the region where a customer’s private key can be unwrapped, because TLS traffic can only be decrypted where that key is available.During initialization, the edge key service (the component on each Cloudflare edge server that unwraps customer private keys and uses them to serve requests) verifies that it has loaded every regional root key required by its configuration. If a configured key is missing or malformed, the service does not start. After initialization, an individual request also fails closed (Cloudflare rejects it rather than risk unwrapping a key out of region) if its metadata identifies a regional root key that is not locally available. If a request for Germany was somehow trying to decrypt in Spain or France it would fail, since neither Spain nor France have the regional root key for Germany. This guarantees that a regional root key never leaves its region, no matter what.Cloudflare needs to maintain high performance while keeping our customers’ regionalized data secure at scale. This is where the next version of GeoKey Manager comes in. We are enabling fast performance while logically separating our network by using post-quantum cryptography to restrict where customers’ private keys are unwrapped. Most of our regions will be available for customers to regionalize their workflow, and there may be product specific caveats. Customers select a region and Cloudflare manages everything else needed to unwrap their private keys within the region’s boundary.How GeoKey Manager ensures that keys are only available in a regionGeoKey Manager controls where wrapped private keys can be unwrapped and used on the data plane. It does not control where requests are forwarded or routed (that’s Regional Services), where tunnels terminate, or where traffic inspection happens (also Regional Services).GeoKey Manager separates globally distributed wrapped private keys from the regional root key required to unwrap it. Quicksilver, our global configuration distribution system, distributes wrapped private keys and its metadata across our network. It does not distribute regional root keys; that happens through a separate provisioning service that stores regional root keys and delivers them only to edge servers authorized for each region. Regional root keys follow a separate, controlled path. On the data plane, a node’s regional configuration, which region a node belongs to, determines which nodes can receive which regional root keys.Defining key hierarchy and application-specific keysEvery wrapped customer private key carries metadata identifying its service context, regional boundary, and epoch.The service context is the Cloudflare service that uses the key, such as Tunnel or Gateway. The regional boundary is the approved set of Cloudflare data centers where the key may be unwrapped and used, such as data centers in Germany or the European Union. The epoch identifies which generation of the regional root key the key belongs to; each rotation creates a new epoch. For example, Acme Co. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (acme0001) and another for Gateway in Germany (acme0002). Road Runner Inc. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (runner0001) and another for Gateway in the European Union (runner0002).Keys with the same service context, regional boundary, and epoch use the same application-specific key pair. Therefore, compromising the Tunnel-Germany application-specific private key could expose both acme0001 and runner0001, but not the Gateway keys. Compromising the Germany regional root key could affect every application-specific key derived from that root for the same epoch, including acme0001, acme0002, and runner0001.In the current architecture, the application-specific key pair is asymmetric. The public component wraps the customer's private key material, while the private component is required to unwrap it. The resulting wrapped private key is distributed with its service context (Access, Gateway, Tunnel, Cloudflare One client), region, and epoch.Provisioning regional root keysWhen Cloudflare/Admin configures a region for a CF1 use case, key management service (which also derives application-specific key pairs and wraps customer private keys) creates a regional root key and associates it with a regional boundary and epoch and sends it to provisioning service for storage and distribution which under the hood uses Vault, which is managed by us on-premises.Authorizing edge servers for a regionBefore an edge server can receive a regional root key, provisioning service evaluates three inputs:Trusted Platform Module (TPM) proves that the server possesses a registered hardware identityZinc, Cloudflare's server inventory system, maps that identity to a data center and location Provisioning service determines which regional root keys the server may accessZinc updates its membership records for each edge server. This asynchronous process adds new servers as the network grows and removes servers when they are decommissioned. As Cloudflare performs maintenance on data centers in Germany, the definition of which data centers belong in Germany changes in Zinc. That definition is swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver so that our edge is up to date. The reverse also works. As we add capacity to our network, the definition of Germany, or any other region, is updated in Zinc and that is also swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver.Zinc also associates a registered hardware identity with a server and physical location, which supports FIPS 140-3 compliance. TPM-backed identity, server inventory data, and regional configurations determine which region an edge server belongs to and what regional root keys it can access.Each edge server calls the control plane’s provisioning service, and provides its registered hardware identity. After verifying the server’s hardware identity and regional membership, the provisioning service issues a token that permits the server to retrieve only the regional root keys authorized for its location. Each edge server receives its token and uses it to fetch the regional root keys.Authorized edge servers load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than persisting them on disk. Process level access controls limit which services can use them. Because this memory is volatile, a machine restart removes the keys and the server must authenticate and provision them again. This adds operational complexity in exchange for reducing persistent key material which could be an attack vector for adversaries.Wrapping private keys for global distributionWhen the key-management service receives a customer's private key material with a service context and regional boundary, it will use the request’s regional boundary to get the regional root key and its latest configured epoch. It will then derive the corresponding asymmetric application key pair and use its public component to wrap the private key. The result is a wrapped private key and its metadata.Quicksilver will then distribute the wrapped private key and metadata across our network. Since the wrapped key requires the specified region to decrypt, global wrapped key distribution does not grant edge servers global access to the private key because unwrapping still requires the corresponding regional root key and service context.Unwrapping using application-specific keys on the data planeWhy we chose this cryptographic designSymmetric roots with asymmetric key wrappingRegional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets. GeoKey Manager derives application-specific keys from each regional root key. For the current Cloudflare One path, the control plane’s key management service derives an application-specific Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) key pair.HPKE with hybrid post-quantum KEMThe Cloudflare One path uses HPKE, as defined in RFC 9180. Its key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combines ML-KEM-768 with X25519, while HKDF-SHA-256 provides key derivation and AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption. Combining post-quantum and classical components preserves confidentiality as long as at least one component remains secure.Designing for rotation The validated design supports two types of key rotation: soft rotation and hard rotation.A soft rotation creates a new epoch for the regional root key while retaining controlled access to a limited number of previous regional root-key epochs — let’s say one previous generation, as an example. The customer’s new private-key material is wrapped using the latest epoch, while older wrapped private keys are still usable during the transition. This is a similar concept to when a credit card company allows you to use a previous version of your credit card for recurring payments from an authorized retailer. In this case, the number of epochs we support determine how many generations of previously wrapped private keys — credit cards — are usable. This allows customers to preserve their service uptime while they transition.A hard rotation instead rewraps affected customers’ wrapped private keys under a replacement epoch so access to the previous epoch can be removed. In this case, it would be like the credit card company not allowing you to use the previous credit card for a transaction under any circumstances.Security and availability tradeoffsFailing closed is a very intentional design choice. Failing open would mean unwrapping a customer’s private key outside its allowed region rather than rejecting the request. We never do that: if any required check fails (service context, region, epoch, etc.), the request is rejected. At startup, each edge’s key service loads every configured regional root key from its Linux kernel keyring. Missing or malformed root keys prevent the edge key service from initializing. Once running, the edge key service uses in-memory copies so that it can’t be tampered with, preventing out of region or cross-region unwrapping. In practice, an edge server serves requests for a region only once its configuration and key provisioning are complete.The trust boundary (all services that can access the regional root key) includes the key-management service, the provisioning service, and authorized edge key services because each can access regional root keys. The key-management service uses them to derive application-specific keys, the provisioning service stores and distributes them, and edge key services use locally authorized copies of them. Quicksilver remains outside this boundary because it receives only wrapped private keys and associated metadata.Operating GeoKey ManagerCloudflare’s network is constantly changing. As servers enter or leave service, Cloudflare’s fleet inventory updates regional membership. This means the list of data centers that make up a region like Spain is not static. GeoKey Manager’s provisioning layer refreshes that membership several times each day, granting or removing access to regional root keys as the network changes. This process is separate from key rotation and requires no customer action.When regional membership changes, the provisioning service immediately synchronizes the server’s Linux kernel keyring with the latest authorized regional root keys. The edge key service caches these keys in process memory until it restarts or the cache expires. It then reloads the current authorized set from the kernel keyring.What’s next: Cloudflare One integration and CDNGeoKey Manager is the basis for an improved Regional Services offering for Cloudflare One; these new capabilities will be announced in a few months.Older versions of GeoKey Manager already provide geographic controls for private keys associated with CDN certificates. We are developing a separate integration that will bring this new post-quantum GeoKey Manager described here to that existing CDN capability. We will share testing and transition details when that work is ready.Getting startedIf you are a current DLS customer who is regionalizing CDN traffic, you can register intent to test this feature before it’s generally available for CDN traffic here.Thank you to everyone who made this product a reality. It was a huge effort across the Data Localization Suite, Cloudflare One, and Cloudflare Research teams.

title: [Netflix] Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
summary: Serdar Cellat, Yuchen Xie, Bernadette Marcu, Blaid Burgess, Cody Jarrett, Carlos Pereira, Qing Shi, Samuel Carvajal, Manuel Pamplona, Dorothy Jung, Feiko Ritsema, Benjamin Klein, Alex Woo, Eugene Lok, Anna Pulido, Rebecka Swe, Sanford Holsapple, Ranjith Kumar ShettyIntroductionClips in the Netflix mobile app.At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips, our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort.Our Video Resizing ApproachConverting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot.We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead.An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios.Shot Detection and SplittingFirst, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles.Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop.Focus Region DiscoveryOnce shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera.Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing.Temporal ReframingOnce we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic.The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path.Tooling and Workflow IntegrationWe integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The interface enables them to automatically generate multiple aspect‑ratio versions of a clip with smart reframing. A unified in‑app module provides intuitive shot‑reframing controls, allowing users to review the algorithm’s crops, and quickly make targeted adjustments where needed.For more complex shots or custom campaigns, producers can export the resizing parameters as XML and load them directly into external timeline editors such as Adobe Premiere. This allows agencies and external partners to start from the algorithm’s framing decisions instead of recreating crops manually or relying on tools like Premiere’s Auto Reframe. In our internal test, our resizing algorithm outperforms Auto Reframe on a curated evaluation set, so the XML export effectively brings those higher‑quality crops into external workflows. By bringing automated resizing and manual refinement into a single place, this pipeline significantly reduces production time and manual effort while preserving creative control.Video resizing interface with reframing controlsConclusionOur work on multi-ratio video resizing is one step in a broader effort to make content creation more scalable, without compromising creative intent. By pairing algorithm-driven reframing with editor-friendly tools, we’ve reduced the time teams spend on repetitive resizing tasks and unlocked faster experimentation across mobile feeds and marketing campaigns. As we continue to broaden these capabilities to new formats and workflows, our goal remains the same: to give creatives more time to tell great stories, and to deliver a consistently high-quality viewing experience for our members and fans.Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform TeamQuasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decisionAt Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:Does any consumer still call this method?Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:What changed in the library’s public API?Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.From API Changes to Consumer ImpactExisting techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.Consider this simplified API change:public interface Client {- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);}For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind, r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_pathFROM requested_changes cJOIN quasar.symbol_refs r ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonicalrequested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.Bringing the Analysis Before ReleaseVersion-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:{ "change": "REMOVED", "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)", "affectedRepositories": 137, "versionDistribution": , "sampleConsumerLocations":  }, { "repository": "client-wrapper", "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java", "lines":  } ], "libraryCriticality": { "tier": 1, "basis": "highest-tier downstream application" }, "comparison": { "baseShaFound": true, "headShaFound": true }}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceedA Polyglot Foundation with SCIPThe shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.Moving Risk Assessment EarlierToday, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.What We LearnedBuilding this workflow led us to four practical lessons.Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possibleRelated TalksFrom Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Scale reservoir uncertainty analysis with agile reservoir modeling
summary: Turn subsurface uncertainty into decision-ready insight Drilling campaigns are among the most expensive and operationally complex activities in the energy industry. Rigs, crews, equipment, and logistics are scheduled months in advance, leaving little room for delay. Every hour of downtime can carry significant costs. Geoscientists and engineers rely on reservoir models to understand the subsurface and guide drilling decisions, often under intense time pressure. Yet the current modeling infrastructure that many companies rely on for these critical decisions was designed for smaller datasets, simpler workflows, and siloed operations. As subsurface data grows in scale and complexity, teams need a faster, more connected way to transform uncertainty into actionable decisions. Now generally available, agile reservoir modeling (ARM) from SLB, integrated with Azure Data Manager for Energy (ADME), is co-engineered for cloud scale to close that gap. The combined solution connects ensemble-centric reservoir modeling and simulation with a governed data foundation, elastic Azure high-performance computing, and scalable storage designed for the throughput and concurrency of large ensemble studies. Learn more about Azure Data Manager for Energy Scale ensemble modeling with ARM on Azure A single reservoir model represents one plausible interpretation of the subsurface. Ensemble modeling evaluates hundreds of model realizations together, giving asset teams a broader view of potential outcomes and a stronger basis for understanding uncertainty and risk. The industry has long recognized the value of ensemble modeling for risk-aware decision-making, but adoption has been constrained by infrastructure and software designed for smaller, sequential studies. Moving from a limited model set to hundreds of realizations multiplies the compute, storage, data movement, and results that must be managed. ARM addresses this barrier by distributing realization generation and simulation across elastic Azure high-performance computing, while scalable storage provides the capacity, throughput, and parallel access required by ensembles of different sizes. When these pieces are fragmented, customers must connect and orchestrate them on their own, and large-scale simulation becomes a disconnected, one-off exercise. SLB and Microsoft combined their respective technologies, ARM engineered by SLB and ADME engineered by Microsoft, to remove that burden. Rather than a set of loosely connected tools, customers get one integrated workflow in which each component has a clear role: Azure Data Manager for Energy is the governed data foundation. OSDU® Technical Standard-aligned services and OSDU Domain Data Management Services (DDMS) manage seismic, wellbore, interpretation, and simulation data. Petrel™ subsurface software is where engineers define interpretation and uncertainty workflows, connected directly to data in ADME. Agile reservoir modeling is the ensemble workflow engine. It orchestrates the generation of reservoir realizations and simulation runs and supports discovery and analysis at enterprise scale. As a result, teams build ensembles from trusted corporate data and publish results back for discovery and reuse, which reduces data movement and improves collaboration across asset teams. Put ensemble modeling into practice with a connected workflow Beyond integration and scale, ARM distinguishes itself by orchestrating all stages of an ensemble study across modeling, simulation, data management, and analysis. The workflow tightly connects the tools reservoir teams already use with Azure-scale infrastructure and the governed data services provided by Azure Data Manager for Energy. ARM generates the realizations, prepares the simulation cases, and coordinates their execution across the Azure environment. Azure high-performance computing executes multiple realizations in parallel. A shared, high-performance Azure Files volume holds model inputs, grids, simulation decks, temporary files, and results so the simulation fleet can read and write concurrently. Because compute capacity, storage capacity, throughput, and IOPS can be scaled independently, the environment can be sized for the concurrency of the ensemble rather than the constraints of fixed infrastructure. As simulations complete, SLB reservoir engineering services manage the resulting ensembles and use OSDU search capabilities on ADME to support discovery, filtering, and sorting across large studies. Teams can locate relevant realizations and supported, published results without manually navigating disconnected project stores. Engineers can analyze ensembles in the reservoir engineering workspace or load them back into Petrel software for further interpretation, history matching, and reservoir engineering studies. This allows teams to work in the environment and application best suited to each task while maintaining continuity, without having to step outside their workflow to manage orchestration. ADME provides entitlement-based access control integrated with Microsoft Entra ID and supports compliance controls such as OSDU legal tags. Connecting ARM workflows to this governed data foundation helps maintain consistent access and compliance as corporate subsurface data is used across modeling and simulation. Because ARM workflows are integrated through Petrel software in ADME, reservoir engineers can perform ensemble-scale studies leveraging their corporate-wide data stores and publish results for discovery, eliminating friction and driving collaboration. Microsoft and SLB engineering collaborated closely to build the integration between Petrel software and ARM for enterprise-scale performance. For reservoir engineers and asset teams, ARM turns ensemble modeling into a repeatable workflow rather than a bespoke infrastructure project. Teams can stress-test development concepts against calibrated ensembles that honor observed production history, not simply run a larger number of models. As new wells are drilled and new data becomes available, they can update their reservoir understanding without waiting for a major model rebuild. For energy IT and data leaders, the workflow connects simulation to an OSDU standard-aligned architecture with consistent identity, governance, search, and interoperability, reducing isolated data copies and disconnected applications. The future of the reservoir lifecycle Building on this partnership, Microsoft and SLB are working within the OSDU community to advance a more cloud-native standard for reservoir data. This work will help models, simulation results, and engineering workflows operate more consistently across applications, improving interoperability while reducing dependence on proprietary formats and silos. A shared, governed data foundation also paves the way for AI and agentic experiences that can discover data, coordinate workflows, and surface insights across the reservoir lifecycle. Combined with Azure-scale compute and storage, this creates a path toward more automated and continuous reservoir modeling.
