title: [GitLab] Extend GitLab Duo Agent Platform into your business systems
summary:
Developers mostly use GitLab Duo Agent Platform where they already work: the IDE, merge requests, and issues. But DevSecOps teams also support the business systems the rest of the company runs on, and those systems break too.In Salesforce, for example, when a validation fails, a callout times out, or a null slips through a trigger, the error gets logged, but the log doesn’t explain the cause. An engineer still has to read the stack trace, find the class in the repository, check what changed recently, and decide whether this is a one-off or a regression. Meanwhile, the business user who hit the error has to wait.When your Salesforce metadata lives in GitLab and ships through GitLab CI/CD, the code that explains the error is already there. In this tutorial, Salesforce calls a custom GitLab Duo Agent Platform flow through the Flows API the moment an error happens. The flow investigates the code, and your team gets a GitLab issue that already contains the root-cause analysis.Along the way, three parts of the GitLab platform work together: GitLab Duo Agent Platform investigates the error, a GitLab issue tracks the work, and GitLab CI/CD runs the flow and ships the fix.Salesforce is the example we’ll walk through in this tutorial, but the same approach works for any system that can make an HTTP request.What you'll buildSalesforce makes one call to GitLab. A custom flow in GitLab Duo Agent Platform does the rest.Errors reach GitLab Duo Agent Platform automatically from your Apex error handling, or on demand from a button. Either way, the same Apex job calls the Flows API, and the flow opens an issue with its analysis.PrerequisitesGitLab Premium or Ultimate, on GitLab.com or GitLab 19.5 and later. The Flows API used in this tutorial is generally available from 19.5.GitLab Duo Agent Platform turned on, with custom flows allowed for your top-level group.Your Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) stored in a GitLab project. This is the project the flow will read.A Maintainer or Owner role in that project.In Salesforce, permission to create a Named Credential, a custom metadata type, and Apex classes.Your Salesforce deployments must be running through a GitLab CI/CD pipeline, so the fix can ship from the same issue.Step 1: Write the triage flowStart in GitLab, because Salesforce will need the flow's ID later.A custom flow is one YAML file in the flow registry v1 syntax. This one has a single agent. When Salesforce starts the flow, it sends the error details as the flow's goal. The agent reads them as context:goal, investigates the repository, and opens one issue.version: "v1" environment: ambient components: - name: "sf_error_triage" type: AgentComponent prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt" inputs: - from: "context:project_id" as: "project_id" - from: "context:goal" as: "error_report" toolset: - "find_files" # locate the class or Flow in the repository - "grep" - "read_file" - "list_commits" # find recent changes to that file - "create_issue" # the only write: open the triage issue prompts: - prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt" prompt_template: system: | You triage Salesforce runtime errors for a team that keeps its Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) in this project. You receive an error report with a class name, exception type, message and stack trace. 1. Find the source file for the class or Flow named in the report. 2. Read the code around the lines in the stack trace. 3. List recent commits that touched that file and identify any change that plausibly introduced the error. 4. Create one issue: - Title: " <exception type> in <class>" - Label: salesforce-error - Description: the original error, then sections for Likely cause, Affected component, Suspect change, Suggested next step, and Confidence (high, medium or low, with one line of reasoning). Rules: - Cite file paths, line numbers and commit SHAs for every claim. - If you cannot find the code or a suspect commit, say so. Do not guess. - Do not change code. A person decides what happens next. user: | Project ID: {{project_id}} Error report: {{error_report}} placeholder: history routers: - from: "sf_error_triage" to: "end" flow: entry_point: "sf_error_triage" The toolset is deliberately narrow: four tools read and one creates an issue. The flow can't push code or change existing issues, which makes it easy to review and easy to trust.Two lines in the prompt do the most work. Requiring a citation for every claim lets an engineer check the reasoning in a minute. Allowing "not found" stops the agent from inventing a cause.To create the flow, go to your project, select AI > Flows > New flow, choose Flow, paste the YAML, and select Create flow. You can also build and test it in VS Code with the GitLab flow builder.Step 2: Enable the flow and get its consumer IDA flow must be enabled in a project before anything can run it.In your project, select AI > Flows, open the Managed tab, and select your flow.Select Enable and choose the project that holds your Salesforce code. GitLab creates a service account for the flow, named ai-<flow>-<group>. The flow runs with a composite identity, so it can never access more than the user who starts it. When Salesforce starts the flow through the API, GitLab runs it as this service account.You don't need a mention or assign trigger. Salesforce will start this flow through the API.To start a custom flow through the API, Salesforce passes the flow's ai_catalog_item_consumer_id. Look it up with a short GraphQL query from the docs, and use the number at the end of the returned gid://gitlab/AiCatalogItemConsumer/<number>. Note it, along with the project ID.Finally, create a project access token with the api scope and at least the Developer role. Salesforce will use it to call GitLab. With a lower role, the API refuses to run catalog flows.Step 3: Call the flow from SalesforceStore the token in a Named Credential. Create a Named Credential called GitLab_API with the URL https://gitlab.com, backed by an External Credential that sends your project access token in the PRIVATE-TOKEN header. The token never appears in code.Call the Flows API from a Queueable. Salesforce doesn't allow callouts in the middle of saving a record, so the call runs as a background job. The job turns the exception into the flow's goal and starts the flow:public with sharing class DuoTriageJob implements Queueable, Database.AllowsCallouts { private final String goal; public DuoTriageJob(Exception e, String className) { goal = 'Class: ' + className + '
Exception: ' + e.getTypeName() + '
Message: ' + e.getMessage() + '
Stack trace:
' + e.getStackTraceString(); } public void execute(QueueableContext ctx) { Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt cfg = Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt.getInstance('Default'); HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest(); req.setEndpoint('callout:GitLab_API/api/v4/ai/duo_workflows/workflows'); req.setMethod('POST'); req.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json'); req.setBody(JSON.serialize(new Map<String, Object>{ 'project_id' => cfg.Project_Id__c, 'ai_catalog_item_consumer_id' => cfg.Consumer_Id__c.intValue(), 'goal' => goal, 'start_workflow' => true, 'allow_agent_to_request_user' => false, 'agent_privileges' => new List<Integer>{ 1, 2, 3 }, 'pre_approved_agent_privileges' => new List<Integer>{ 1, 2, 3 } })); HttpResponse res = new Http().send(req); // 201 Created: the response includes web_url, a link to the agent session. } } The project ID and consumer ID from Step 2 live in a custom metadata type, Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt, so you can change them without a deployment.Three settings in the request body do the most work:allow_agent_to_request_user: false means the flow runs to completion without pausing for questions. Nobody is watching a Salesforce error at 2 a.m.agent_privileges limits the agent to reading files (1), reading GitLab (2), and writing to GitLab (3), which it needs to create the issue. It can't run commands or use Git. List all privileges to check the IDs on your instance.pre_approved_agent_privileges repeats the same list, so the flow never stops to wait for tool approval.This example leaves out response checks, retries, and tests. Add them before you go to production.Step 4: Start the flow automatically or on demandAutomatically. Queue the job wherever your code catches and handles an exception:try { OpportunityDiscountService.applyTierDiscount(opportunities); } catch (Exception e) { System.enqueueJob(new DuoTriageJob(e, 'OpportunityDiscountService')); // ...your existing error handling } If the whole transaction is rolled back, Salesforce discards the queued job too, so place the call where your code handles the error and carries on.On demand. Some teams would rather choose which errors are worth investigating. Wrap the job in an invocable Apex action, label it Ask GitLab Duo to investigate, and add it to a screen flow that runs as a quick action on the record where you keep errors, such as a log record or a support case. One click in Salesforce, and the issue appears in GitLab a few minutes later.Step 5: What your team seesA user saves an Opportunity, an Apex trigger throws, and a few minutes later a new issue appears in the GitLab project. Here is an illustrative example of what the flow writes:##  System.NullPointerException in OpportunityDiscountService Label: salesforce-error ### Original error Attempt to de-reference a null object Class.OpportunityDiscountService.applyTierDiscount: line 48, column 1 Trigger.OpportunityTrigger: line 12, column 1 ### Likely cause applyTierDiscount() reads opp.Account.Tier__c without a null check (line 48). Opportunities saved without an Account reach this line with opp.Account == null. ### Affected component force-app/main/default/classes/OpportunityDiscountService.cls, called from OpportunityTrigger (before update). ### Suspect change Commit 3f9c2ab, "Apply tier discount on stage change", added the Tier__c lookup. Before that commit, the method returned early when AccountId was blank. ### Suggested next step Restore the early return for a blank AccountId, or guard the lookup. Add a test that updates an Opportunity with no Account. ### Confidence High. The stack trace line matches the new code in 3f9c2ab. Nothing in Salesforce or the codebase changed. The flow did the first round of investigation and left the decision to an engineer: fix it now, schedule it, or close it as expected behavior.The Flows API response includes a web_url for the agent session. Open it to see each step the flow took, which is the fastest way to tune the prompt.Guardrails for productionBefore you run this in production, check these points. They decide whether the pattern holds up under real traffic.Send the shape of the error, not the data. Strip record IDs, emails, and free text that may hold customer data from the message before it leaves Salesforce. Review what the goal contains with your security team before you turn this on.Grant the fewest privileges. Reading files, reading GitLab, and creating an issue are enough. Expand the flow, for example to open merge requests, only after it has earned trust with accurate analysis.Scope the token. Use a project access token for one project, not a personal token, and rotate it on a schedule.Keep a person in charge. The flow investigates; an engineer decides. Citations in every issue let the engineer verify the reasoning instead of redoing it.One platform, from error to fixFollow that error from start to finish:GitLab Duo investigates it. The flow reads the stack trace, finds the code, and points to the change that most likely caused the error.A GitLab issue tracks it. The analysis becomes work the team can label, prioritize, assign, and plan into a milestone, like any other issue.GitLab CI/CD runs it and ships the fix. The flow itself runs on GitLab CI/CD, and so does your Salesforce deployment pipeline. An engineer opens a merge request from the issue, the pipeline validates and deploys the change to Salesforce, and the issue closes when the merge request merges.Because every step happens in GitLab, the trail stays connected. The issue links to the merge request, the merge request to its pipeline, and the pipeline to the deployment. Anyone can see what broke, why, who fixed it, and when the fix reached production.Beyond Salesforce errorsStrip away the Salesforce details and the pattern is simple: a business system makes one HTTP call, and a custom GitLab Duo flow that knows your code does the investigation. Any system that can send a request can start a flow.Here are a few ideas for where the same pattern could help:A failed sync in an ERP integration, traced to the mapping code that last changed.A support case tagged "possible bug," checked against recent releases before it reaches an engineer.A failed scheduled data job, matched to the last change in its pipeline definition.For DevSecOps teams, this means errors from the business systems they support arrive as issues with a likely cause attached, not as raw logs to trace manually. Business teams don't need to learn GitLab, and engineers don't need to watch another dashboard. Each system keeps doing its job, and GitLab Duo Agent Platform gives engineering a head start every time something breaks.Try it yourselfPick one business system your team supports and one error it logs today. Give a custom flow the code, call it from that system, and see what the first analysis tells you. Start a free trial of GitLab Duo Agent Platform, or if you're already on GitLab Premium or Ultimate, turn on Duo Agent Platform and build your first custom flow.Further readingFlows APICustom flowsCustom flow YAML schemaComposite identityGitLab Duo Agent Platform: complete getting started guide

title: [GitLab] Redesign how your team ships software with AI agents
summary: AI agents are sending more and more code into review queues built for human-paced work. A coding assistant can speed up code writing, but it can’t show you whether review, security checks, and release approvals can keep pace with all that extra code. AI-native engineering — the practice of intentionally designing the engineering process so people and agents each do what they are best suited to — starts with identifying delivery bottlenecks, then deciding how much autonomy agents should have and how to maintain control as you scale.The AI-Native Engineering Playbook, launching this week, helps teams turn faster coding into faster delivery by redesigning how they ship software with agents. Every practice in the playbook is grounded in insights from engineering leaders at GitLab, our customers, and members of our Software Engineering Leadership Forum (SELF) community. We also partnered with IT Revolution to incorporate findings from a diverse group of practitioners looking at AI-native software development from a number of different angles, from code review to agent autonomy.Below are a few of the questions we sought to answer in the process of creating the playbook.Where does the bottleneck go when coding gets faster?Coding used to be the slowest, most expensive part of building software. Agents removed the bottleneck on coding, and the constraint moved to everything around the code: waiting for clarifications, environments, approvals, and other teams. GitLab’s AI Accountability Report, based on an April 2026 survey of 1,528 DevSecOps professionals, found that 79% of respondents agreed that individual developer productivity has improved with AI, but the overall software delivery process has not accelerated at the same pace.Large enterprises typically have software delivery lead times of well over 200 days, with active development taking only 10% to 20% of that time. The numbers explain why a faster coding step is often disappointing in the long run. For example, imagine a 281-day delivery cycle that involves about 32 days spent on coding. Make coding 50% faster, and you save about 16 days, a 6% improvement. But if you take coding all the way to zero, around 88% of the lead time stays untouched. GitLab’s research similarly found that DevSecOps professionals reported spending only 16% of their time writing new code, and 85% agreed AI has shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.That means your first job is diagnosis. Take one small, real change and trace it from request to production, marking every wait and every handoff. The longest waits show where your next improvement is, and it's rarely in the code. Watch where an agent stalls on a small task, too. The stall usually points to a standard nobody documented, an environment that’s hard to start, or context that lived in a single person’s head.How much autonomy should agents have?Agent autonomy should depend on how well you can verify the agent output. Imagine a ladder with four stages, ranging from semi-manual (a person approving every step) to fully autonomous (a zero-touch workflow). In this framework, there are clear rules for advancing up the ladder: no rungs can be skipped, and each step up needs to be backed with evidence from the rung below. Stage 1: Humans are in the loop at every stepStage 2: Humans are still in the loop, but the agent executes within set boundsStage 3: Humans are out of the loop for normal operation and handle only exceptionsStage 4: A zero-touch workflow, where the agent manages itself end to end, calling in a human only when predefined thresholds are met It’s also important for a named human to stay accountable for every AI-enabled workflow, and the line between a human reviewing and a human monitoring should be explicitly defined, since loose or arbitrary definitions tend to erode under time pressure. That erosion is the trap. A person who is nominally in the loop but approves everything gives the appearance of control without the benefits, and habit and volume can easily turn review into mindless rubber-stamping. A checkpoint nobody actually exercises is worse than none, because it creates confidence where the system needs scrutiny.The way up is to earn each step on evidence. Set an explicit accuracy or success threshold before you widen a step, then move people from reviewing each step to monitoring the whole. An agent that stops more often to ask for help is a healthy sign, since the system is refusing to outrun its own evidence. How do you review code at agent volume?Widening autonomy depends on catching mistakes, and that puts pressure on code review. Review at merge time was built for human-paced output. Agents raise the rate of change, and manual review of every change set has become unsustainable. GitLab’s research also highlighted this strain: 78% of respondents agreed existing code review processes were not designed for the scale of code AI tools enable, and 80% agreed their organization has adopted AI coding tools faster than it has developed policies to govern them.The answer is a layered verification system in which each layer does the part it does best. Humans are only removed from the loop when the risk level and evidence justify that design choice — it’s never a default. Move objective checks, such as formatting, types, and dependency policy, as close to authoring as possible.Keep changes small so every later layer works faster.Define the expected behavior up front so there is something concrete to check.Use an independent reviewer.Match review depth to the risk of the change.Record every agentic review decision in a form someone can inspect later.The organizations that have been most successful here have already invested heavily in automated testing, static analysis, and small change sets, so the layers work best on a foundation you already have. Dive into the playbook, or contribute your own insightsBecoming AI-native is a practice that leaders will continue to refine with their teams as tools and understanding evolve. To get started, read the entire playbook, or begin with the part that matches where your team runs into the most friction:Redesigning the work so agents fit the flow of delivery instead of attaching to steps built for people aloneWorking with agents by deciding where human judgment and accountability stay and how engineers keep growing as the coding shiftsGoverning and scaling from one workflow to many with the context, verification, and measurement that let you move faster without losing control of quality or riskIf you lead an engineering team and want to contribute your own insights to the playbook, join SELF, the community for engineering leaders navigating the AI era.Papers cited in this articleCochran, Timothy, and Bryan Finster, Tim Ottersburg, Scott Prugh, and Amy Willard. title: [Sentry] Sentry JavaScript SDK v11 adds tracing for all JS platforms
summary: This post is about a recent change to the Sentry JavaScript SDKs. If you don't use Sentry with JavaScript, it may still be useful as a look at how we made the change and why. In the Sentry JavaScript SDK v11, we rebuilt how our tracing integrations work. While we still support the OpenTelemetry standard (described in more detail below), we now instrument your dependencies with a code transformer instead of using the OpenTelemetry instrumentation classes as we did in previous versions. This approach is built on the apm-js-collab packages @apm-js-collab/code-transformer and @apm-js-collab/tracing-hooks, a shared effort across application performance monitoring (APM) vendors. Injection & subscription The new tracing instrumentations work in two parts. The first injects diagnostics channels into a module as it's being loaded, and the second listens on those channel events to gather tracing information to send to Sentry. Part 1: injection When a supported module is loaded, either at runtime or as part of a bundler job, the transform rewrites the source to wrap the functions we care about in a tracingChannel() call. Each transform is driven by a config that names the package, a semver range, a file inside the package, and a function: { channelName: 'query', module: { name: 'mysql', versionRange: '>=2.0.0 <3', filePath: 'lib/Connection.js', }, functionQuery: { expressionName: 'query', kind: 'Auto' }, } Once transformed, the mysql module now publishes start, end, error, asyncStart, and asyncEnd diagnostics whenever the query function is called. Part 2: subscription Each Sentry integration (mysqlIntegration, redisIntegration, openAIIntegration, and so on) subscribes to its channels and turns the events into Sentry spans. The subscriber holds off until it hears that its module is actually loaded, to avoid creating excess channels. Injection at run time & build time The same transform runs in two places, and both can be active at once. Either a module is loaded as part of a bundler, or from node_modules, but not both, so there's no chance of double-wrapping. At run time In recent Node versions, and in Deno 2.8.3 and up, Sentry.init() calls registerDiagnosticsChannelInjection() automatically, which will use the Module.registerHooks API to instrument any supported modules loaded after that point. You can also register the hooks before your app loads at all, by using the import endpoints provided in the Deno and Node SDKs: node --import @sentry/node/import app.js deno run --preload=@sentry/deno/import app.ts At build time If you are using bun build, or bundling your program using a bundler like Vite or esbuild, you can use the provided plugins to instrument modules as they are built into the application. @sentry/node ships plugins for Vite, Rollup, webpack, and esbuild; @sentry/cloudflare includes one for Vite; @sentry/bun ships one for bun build; Next.js wires the webpack loader into both webpack and Turbopack. The plugin transforms each instrumented dependency as it is bundled, and splices in a snippet that registers the module (and its subscriber factory) on a global marker when the bundled module is first evaluated. Usage is the same as any other Sentry bundler plugin: // vite.config.ts plugins: , }; The approach before v11 Before v11, Sentry's integrations were almost entirely based on the OpenTelemetry instrumentation APIs. This let us use work from the open source community, but it also had significant drawbacks that grew worse as more JavaScript platforms gained popularity. Inside an OpenTelemetry instrumentation An OpenTelemetry instrumentation package, such as @opentelemetry/instrumentation-express, exports a class that extends InstrumentationBase. It declares a package name, a supported semver range, and a patch(moduleExports, version) function. It can also declare InstrumentationNodeModuleFile entries to only patch individual files inside the package. registerInstrumentations() installs two loader hooks: require-in-the-middle, which patches Module._load for CommonJS. import-in-the-middle, registered through Module.register() as an ECMAScript module (ESM) loader hook. When an instrumented module loads, these loader hooks hand the OpenTelemetry instrumentation the module's exports object and its base directory. The instrumentation reads <baseDir>/package.json off disk to find the version, checks it against the declared range, and calls patch(exports). The patch uses shimmer to replace properties on the exports object in place. The replacement function opens an OpenTelemetry span, and Sentry's SentrySpanProcessor, SentrySampler, and SentryContextManager convert that span into a Sentry span. ESM namespace objects are immutable, so import-in-the-middle cannot simply assign to them. It reads each module's source from disk, lexes the export names (cjs-module-lexer for CommonJS, a source scan for ESM), generates a replacement module that re-exports through mutable local bindings, and wraps the namespace in a Proxy. Only then can shimmer's assignment take effect. A chain of assumptions Each step in this process assumes something about the environment. Together they need: a live module loader that runs a require() or a Node ESM resolve/load hook for every dependency. Node's loader internals, Module._load and Module.register(). the dependency present on disk as its own package directory, with a readable package.json and readable source files. exports that the patch can reassign. the hooks installed before the first import of the library. OpenTelemetry warns when it is too late: "Module x has been loaded before y so it might not work". Limits placed on bundlers After a bundler inlines a dependency, none of those assumptions hold. require('express') becomes a reference to a function defined higher up in the same file, so there is no load event to intercept. There is no node_modules/express/package.json to read, so the version check has nothing to check against. ESM const bindings inside a bundle cannot be reassigned, and a call site may already hold a direct reference to the function before any patch could run. The workarounds pushed the work back to the user: mark every instrumented package as external, ship a node_modules tree next to the bundle, and accept that this undoes much of the reason for bundling. Platforms that bundle your server code for you, such as Vercel and Netlify, left no place to apply that workaround at all. Node.js only Everything about this approach is Node-specific. When Sentry's JS SDK started down this path a few years ago, that was a reasonable restriction, because Node.js was the main server-side JavaScript runtime. As more runtimes became popular, it stopped being reasonable. Cloudflare Workers have no part of the chain at all: no CommonJS loader, no Module.register(), no filesystem to read a package.json from, and module resolution happens at build time in the Workers bundler. Bun and Deno implement much of the user-facing portions of Node's module system, but not Module._load patching, and the older Module.register hooks are empty stub functions on these platforms. Ordering & preloads Because ESM import statements are hoisted and evaluated before any code in the importing file, Sentry.init() in an ESM entry point runs after the libraries it wants to patch have already been loaded. In v10, the options were --import=./instrument.mjs, the @sentry/node/preload entry point, preloadOpenTelemetry(), and a SENTRY_PRELOAD_INTEGRATIONS environment variable for apps that needed the patches installed early but could not configure the SDK yet. Weight Every supported library needed its own @opentelemetry/instrumentation-* package, pinned against that library's internals, and Sentry had to keep the OpenTelemetry SDK present (tracer provider, sampler, span processor, context manager, and propagator) to receive the spans. Fixing these problems in v11 The new approach replaces that entire chain, by injecting tracing channels just like the built-in channels library authors can use: Bundled server deployments just work. A source transform can run during a build, because it modifies the source code, not the resulting object. The bundler plugin instruments dependencies while they are being bundled, which a loader-hook system cannot do at all. This covers Vercel and Netlify, which bundle your server code for you. Non-Node runtimes work. node:diagnostics_channel is built into Node, and is implemented by Bun, Deno, and Cloudflare Workers (with nodejs_compat). This was the main reason for the change. It edits library code, not exports. The transform wraps the function inside the module's own source, so it does not matter whether a package freezes its exports, re-exports through a barrel file, or has been inlined by a bundler. Export object monkey-patching fails in all of those cases. One ordering rule instead of several. A library instruments itself the moment it is loaded, so preloadOpenTelemetry(), @sentry/node/preload, and SENTRY_PRELOAD_INTEGRATIONS are all gone. At runtime, a single registration call covers every library. Less to install, and less to go wrong. The dependency tree is cut back to just @opentelemetry/api, instead of a tree of instrumentation packages, and @sentry/node-core has been folded back into @sentry/node. generateInstrumentOnce(), SentryContextManager, SentrySampler, and SentrySpanProcessor were removed. Sentry stays out of your OpenTelemetry setup. Sentry spans no longer leak into your pipeline, and your pipeline no longer has to use Sentry's context manager and propagator. There's still quite a bit of flexibility in how you can use Sentry with a custom OpenTelemetry setup, as discussed below. This instrumentation, which injects diagnostics channels with a source transform, already existed in v10 behind experimentalUseDiagnosticsChannelInjection(); v11 makes it the default and removes the export-patching instrumentations. Platform coverage Before adopting this approach, we explored quite a few other options. It's a big change, and the open source OpenTelemetry-based instrumentations have a long history of reliable use in production systems. Part of the motivation was to deliver similar OpenTelemetry support to all JavaScript platforms. Node itself is moving its module loader hooks in a different direction, so porting import-in-the-middle and require-in-the-middle to every JS platform did not seem worth the effort. The new approach gave us results on three platforms right away. Cloudflare Workers Workers have no Node module loader, so v10's approach could not attach to anything. Tracing beyond fetch and the request handler meant calling the manual wrappers yourself (for example, instrumentOpenAiClient and the like). v11 adds @sentry/cloudflare/vite. sentryCloudflareVitePlugin() transforms your dependencies as the worker bundle is built, so database drivers and AI clients emit spans inside the worker. The subscriber integrations are registered by the injected snippet rather than imported, so a worker built without the plugin ships none of that code. Bun @sentry/bun/plugin exports sentryBunPlugin() for bun build. Unfortunately, this is build-only for now. Due to a known issue, any module returned by a runtime onLoad plugin in Bun loses its CommonJS named exports (oven-sh/bun#34112), so a runtime hook would break the libraries it instruments. Running unbundled source with bun run therefore gets no channel instrumentation, which we felt was better than partial or broken coverage. The Bun team is working on the issue, so we expect this to be temporary. In the meantime, production systems on Bun often use bun build for optimization anyway. Deno In 2026, Deno greatly improved its diagnostics_channel coverage and its support for module loader hooks, so tracing on Deno now works much like tracing on Node. deno run --preload=@sentry/deno/import registers the runtime hook. Deno's minimum supported version (2.8.3) already has stable synchronous module hooks, so this is the same code path as modern Node. (These are Module.registerHooks(), a different API from the legacy hooks the OpenTelemetry instrumentations use.) @sentry/deno now exports the whole channel integration set, including database connectors, web frameworks, AI provider integrations, and more being added all the time. In v10 it had none of them. Pitfalls & caveats There are a few things to watch for when you upgrade. Every improvement is a change, as they say. The short version: read the migration guide and follow it. Load order still matters. The transform only applies to modules loaded after the hooks are registered. Register through --import, or keep Sentry.init() above every import of an instrumented library. --require is no longer supported. Node re-runs --require preloads on the loader thread that Module.register() spawns, so an instrument file would run Sentry.init() a second time on a thread that would never execute your code. Use --import, which works for CommonJS apps too. Do not externalize instrumented libraries in a build-time setup. An external dependency is loaded from node_modules and never reaches the transform, so its channels are silently never injected. The Sentry build plugin strips known instrumented packages back out of external, and warns about the ones it cannot fix. Verify with debug: true. We designed the system to work without extra setup, but we also planned for the cases where it doesn't. At init() time, the SDK reports whether the runtime hook registered, whether the bundler plugin ran, and which modules each one injected. If you run your test and CI setup with debug: true in your Sentry settings (especially while making changes to your setup), it'll catch most mistakes. Custom OpenTelemetry setups in v11 Instrumentation and OpenTelemetry are now separate concerns. Sentry still works with OpenTelemetry, and the architecture behind it is simpler. Channel integrations create native Sentry spans directly from the channel events, so whichever of the following you pick, your dependencies stay instrumented. skipOpenTelemetrySetup is replaced by enableOpenTelemetrySetup, with the meaning inverted. It defaults to false on most server SDKs and to true on @sentry/nextjs and @sentry/sveltekit, which still register a light tracer provider to pick up the spans those frameworks emit. Option 1: Sentry only (the default) Set tracesSampleRate and you are done. Option 2: OpenTelemetry-compatible mode Set enableOpenTelemetrySetup: true. Sentry registers a minimal tracer provider, context manager, and propagator, so spans created through @opentelemetry/api become native Sentry spans. This is not a general OpenTelemetry pipeline: there is no exporter and no OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) output. Sentry refuses to register its provider if you already registered one, and logs a warning instead. Option 3: Your own OpenTelemetry, with Sentry linked to it Leave enableOpenTelemetrySetup at false, leave tracesSampleRate unset, run your own provider, and add Sentry.otlpIntegration(): const provider = new NodeTracerProvider({ spanProcessors: , }); provider.register(); Sentry.init({ dsn: '__DSN__', integrations: , }); otlpIntegration() attaches Sentry errors, logs, metrics, and crons to whatever OpenTelemetry span is active, so all your telemetry lands in one trace. It sets up no exporter, span processor, or tracer provider, and leaves outgoing propagation to your propagator. If you had a custom setup in v10, the migration points are: There is no longer a way to route spans from your own provider into Sentry as Sentry spans. SentryContextManager, SentrySampler, and SentrySpanProcessor were removed. Export over OTLP instead, and point your exporter at Sentry.getOtlpTracesEndpoint(dsn). otlpIntegration moved. It is exported from the main entry of every server SDK, so @sentry/node-core/light/otlp is gone. setupOtlpTracesExporter and collectorUrl were removed. The integration reports itself as Otlp rather than OtlpIntegration. Watch for duplicate spans. Sentry instruments many of the same libraries you do. Leaving tracesSampleRate unset is the simple answer. If you want Sentry spans alongside your own, filter the overlapping integrations, and use httpIntegration({ spans: false }) and nativeNodeFetchIntegration({ spans: false }) rather than removing them, because httpIntegration also provides request isolation, request data, and session tracking. HTTP and fetch spans changed. In v10, skipOpenTelemetrySetup: true also turned those off. In v11 Sentry emits them whenever tracing is enabled. Resources are no longer collected. contexts.otel.resource was dropped from events, and the SDK no longer reads OTEL_SERVICE_NAME or OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. Upgrading to v11 v11 moves tracing off the OpenTelemetry instrumentation packages and onto source transforms and diagnostics channels. On Node, that means fewer dependencies and one ordering rule instead of several. If you run on Cloudflare Workers, Deno, or Bun (with bun build), or deploy bundled server code to Vercel or Netlify, your dependencies now get automatic tracing where they had little or none before. To upgrade, start with the migration guide, and turn on debug: true the first time you run the new version so you can see which modules were instrumented. The transform and hooks come from the apm-js-collab packages, which we build together with other APM vendors. If something does not work the way you expect, open an issue in the sentry-javascript repository.

title: [Snyk] AI Model Risk Depends on What the Model Can Reach
